subject: biology
title: Four coded foods: evidence before identification
official_title: Identification of starch, non-reducing sugars, reducing sugars, proteins and lipids using simple laboratory tests

source_verification.note: Official handbook activity objectives, materials and method inspected; this original theoretical exercise uses fictional data or specimen features and does not reproduce a laboratory protocol.

scenario: Interpret a fictional teacher-provided results table. Distilled-water negative controls gave their expected negative colours. No reagent preparation or testing is requested.
tasks: Which sample supports the presence of starch?
Which sample supports a non-reducing sugar?
What carbohydrate class is detected in C before hydrolysis?
Which sample supports protein?
Which sample supports lipid?
worked_explanation: A gives the starch–iodine colour. B becomes reducing only after hydrolysis, consistent with a non-reducing sugar such as sucrose. C contains evidence for both reducing sugar and protein; foods can contain multiple classes. Sudan III stains the lipid phase in D. These are qualitative class identifications, not concentration measurements.
common_error: Calling C a pure protein or using colour intensity to calculate an unsupported concentration.
transfer_question: An unknown is Benedict-positive before hydrolysis. Does a positive result afterwards, by itself, establish a non-reducing sugar?
transfer_answer: No. The original reducing sugar can account for the later positive result; the before/after pair alone does not establish an additional non-reducing sugar.

subject: biology
title: Microscope field calibration and focusing
official_title: Identification of parts and functions of the light microscope and the use of light microscope to observe specimens

source_verification.note: Official handbook activity objectives, materials and method inspected; this original theoretical exercise uses fictional data or specimen features and does not reproduce a laboratory protocol.

scenario: A fictional calibrated light microscope shows six similar onion epidermal cells spanning the high-power field without gaps. Treat the field diameter as accurate and use only this row for the size estimate.
tasks: Calculate total high-power magnification.
Estimate one cell length in micrometres.
Name the focusing control appropriate for the final high-power adjustment.
Name the component that changes the objective in use.
Explain why higher magnification need not reveal additional detail.
marks: Resolution limits the ability to distinguish closely spaced structures.
worked_explanation: Total magnification is 10 × 40 = 400. The 0.45 mm field is 450 µm wide, so 450/6 = 75 µm per cell. A larger image is not necessarily a better-resolved image; apparent enlargement and resolving power are distinct.
common_error: Converting 0.45 mm to 45 µm, or using coarse focus for final high-power adjustment.
transfer_question: A cell image measures 24 mm on a drawing and represents a 60 µm cell. What is the drawing magnification?

subject: biology
title: Three electron micrographs: organisation and scale
official_title: Use of electron micrographs to understand the structure of cellular components

source_verification.note: Official handbook activity objectives, materials and method inspected; this original theoretical exercise uses fictional data or specimen features and does not reproduce a laboratory protocol.

data: Cell wall, chloroplasts, large vacuole, membrane-bound nucleus
Membrane-bound nucleus and mitochondria; no cell wall or chloroplast
Cell wall, ribosomes and nucleoid; no membrane-bound nucleus
5.0 µm scale bar printed 20 mm long; chloroplast image 24 mm long
scenario: Feature descriptions stand in for three fictional electron micrographs; no drawings are supplied. Identify the cell types using combinations of positive features.
tasks: Identify P as plant, animal or prokaryotic.
Identify Q as plant, animal or prokaryotic.
Identify R as plant, animal or prokaryotic.
Name the structure supporting aerobic ATP production in Q.
Calculate the actual length of the chloroplast in P.
worked_explanation: P has a plant-cell combination; Q fits an animal cell; R lacks a membrane-bound nucleus and is prokaryotic. Scaling against the bar avoids needing the original image magnification: 24/20 × 5 = 6 µm. Ribosomes occur in all three cell types and are not evidence of eukaryotic organisation.
common_error: Identifying every walled cell as a plant cell.
transfer_question: R is drawn with a 9 mm cell length and a 3 mm scale bar labelled 1 µm. What length does it represent?

subject: biology
title: Chromosome behaviour identifies the division
official_title: Identification of different stages of mitosis and meiosis using microscopic slides

source_verification.note: Official handbook activity objectives, materials and method inspected; this original theoretical exercise uses fictional data or specimen features and does not reproduce a laboratory protocol.

data: Visible chromosome arrangement in a species with 2n = 8
Eight duplicated chromosomes individually at the equator
Four duplicated chromosomes moving towards each pole; centromeres remain joined
Sister chromatids moving apart; each becomes a daughter chromosome
scenario: Panels are fictional chromosome-diagram descriptions. Distinguish homologous chromosome separation from sister-chromatid separation; cell shape is not diagnostic here.
tasks: Name the stage represented by A.
Name the mitotic stage represented by B.
Name the stage represented by C.
What structures separate at anaphase of mitosis, as in D?
How many chromosomes occur in each daughter nucleus immediately after meiosis I?
worked_explanation: Bivalents are paired homologues, so A belongs to meiosis I. Homologues separate in C without centromere division. After meiosis I each nucleus is haploid, n = 4, although its chromosomes still have two sister chromatids. D alone could also fit anaphase II; the task specifies mitosis.
common_error: Counting chromatids as separate chromosomes before their centromeres divide.
transfer_question: In the same species, how many chromosomes would a normal gamete contain after meiosis II?
transfer_answer: 4, each consisting of one chromatid before any subsequent DNA replication.

subject: biology
title: Amylase: endpoint time and relative reaction rate
official_title: Laboratory experiment to demonstrate enzyme activity and to determine the effect of temperature on the rate of enzymatic reaction (starch - amylase)

source_verification.note: Official handbook activity objectives, materials and method inspected; this original theoretical exercise uses fictional data or specimen features and does not reproduce a laboratory protocol.

data: Time until iodine no longer becomes blue-black (min)
scenario: Fictional starch–amylase tests used identical starting volumes, concentrations and pH. Endpoints were checked at two-minute intervals, matching the handbook sampling approach. Reciprocal time is an index of rate, not an absolute molar rate.
tasks: Calculate the relative rate at 25 °C in min⁻¹.
Calculate the ratio of the 40 °C rate to the 25 °C rate.
Which tested temperature gave the fastest observed starch disappearance?
Name one variable, other than temperature, that must be controlled.
Why must the 60 °C result not be entered as an exact zero rate?
marks: pH, or initial starch concentration, or initial amylase concentration (any one).
Failure to reach the endpoint within the observation period does not prove no reaction occurred.
worked_explanation: Use 1/t: 1/8 = 0.125 and 1/4 = 0.25 min⁻¹. Thus the measured rate index doubles from 25 to 40 °C. High temperature can reduce amylase activity through denaturation, but the uncompleted endpoint only supplies an observational limit. Two-minute sampling also limits endpoint precision; 40 °C is the fastest tested condition, not a proven exact optimum.
common_error: Plotting time as if a longer endpoint time meant a faster reaction, or declaring an exact optimum from four temperatures.
transfer_question: A separate test reaches its endpoint in 10 min. What is its reciprocal-time rate index?

subject: biology
title: Audus readings: when more light stops increasing oxygen output
official_title: Determination of rate of photosynthesis by the amount of oxygen released using Audus apparatus(for different CO2 concentrations and light intensities)

source_verification.note: Official handbook activity objectives, materials and method inspected; this original theoretical exercise uses fictional data or specimen features and does not reproduce a laboratory protocol.

scenario: Fictional Audus-apparatus readings use the same aquatic shoot at constant temperature and carbon-dioxide supply. The collected gas is assumed to be oxygen. Distances are treatment labels; no inverse-square law is assumed for this lamp geometry.
tasks: Calculate oxygen output rate at 40 cm.
Between which consecutive distances does output first plateau?
Suggest one factor that could limit output on this plateau.
Why is oxygen volume preferable to bubble count when bubble sizes vary?
Does measured oxygen release directly give gross photosynthesis?
marks: Carbon-dioxide availability, or another limiting factor such as temperature (any one plausible factor).
Volume accounts for unequal bubble sizes whereas a count does not.
No; respiration consumes some oxygen, so release is a net measure under these assumptions.
worked_explanation: The 40 cm reading gives 0.40/5 = 0.080 cm³ min⁻¹. Moving the lamp nearer increases output initially, then the final two readings are equal. A plateau is compatible with another limiting factor; it does not identify that factor uniquely. Constant temperature is important because moving a lamp can also heat the apparatus.
common_error: Calling the plateau proof that carbon dioxide alone was limiting.
transfer_question: At a fixed light treatment a shoot releases 0.84 cm³ in 7 min. Find its output rate.

subject: biology
title: C3 and C4 sections: recognising a structural pattern
official_title: Microscopic observation of cross sections of C3 and C4 plant leaves with special reference to the adaptations for photosynthesis

source_verification.note: Official handbook activity objectives, materials and method inspected; this original theoretical exercise uses fictional data or specimen features and does not reproduce a laboratory protocol.

data: Distinct upper palisade and lower spongy mesophyll; bundle sheath not conspicuously chloroplast-rich
Prominent chloroplast-rich bundle sheath around vascular bundles; mesophyll arranged around that sheath
scenario: Two fictional leaf sections represent the typical C3/C4 patterns used in the handbook comparison. These are representative examples, not a claim that every species follows an identical anatomy.
tasks: Which section shows typical Kranz anatomy?
Which section is the typical C3 example?
Name the chloroplast-rich cells surrounding the vascular bundle in M.
In a typical C4 leaf, in which cell type is CO₂ initially fixed by PEP carboxylase?
What feature of C4 function reduces photorespiration at Rubisco?
marks: Concentration of CO₂ in bundle-sheath cells near Rubisco.
worked_explanation: The diagnostic observation in M is the conspicuous sheath with surrounding mesophyll. Typical C4 photosynthesis separates initial carbon fixation in mesophyll from the Calvin cycle in bundle-sheath cells, increasing local CO₂ availability to Rubisco. L is the representative dorsiventral C3 section in this exercise; palisade tissue alone is not a universal C3 test.
common_error: Assigning C4 status from leaf thickness alone or saying that C4 plants do not use the Calvin cycle.
transfer_question: A new section has chloroplast-rich bundle-sheath cells encircled by mesophyll. What anatomical term describes this arrangement?
transfer_answer: Kranz anatomy; it supports identification as a typical C4 leaf, subject to the stated representative context.

subject: biology
title: Two respirometers: derive CO₂ instead of guessing fuel
official_title: Determination of rate of respiration and respiratory quotient using germinating seeds

source_verification.note: Official handbook activity objectives, materials and method inspected; this original theoretical exercise uses fictional data or specimen features and does not reproduce a laboratory protocol.

data: Germinating seed mass in each vessel
scenario: Two matched airtight respirometers operate at stable temperature and pressure. Control-corrected volume changes are supplied. With absorbent the decrease represents oxygen uptake; without it the decrease represents oxygen uptake minus carbon-dioxide production.
tasks: State oxygen uptake over the run.
Calculate carbon-dioxide production over the run.
Calculate respiratory quotient.
Calculate oxygen uptake per gram per minute.
Does the RQ uniquely identify fat as the respiratory fuel?
marks: No; an RQ of 0.80 is compatible with mixed substrates or protein and does not uniquely prove fat.
worked_explanation: Without absorbent, outgoing CO₂ offsets part of oxygen consumption. Thus CO₂ produced = 1.20 − 0.24 = 0.96 cm³ and RQ = 0.96/1.20 = 0.80. Mass-specific oxygen uptake is 1.20/(25 × 120) = 0.00040 cm³ g⁻¹ min⁻¹. Stable temperature and matched controls matter because gas-volume changes need not otherwise be biological.
common_error: Using the no-absorbent volume decrease directly as CO₂ produced.
transfer_question: A second corrected run uses 2.00 cm³ oxygen and releases 1.40 cm³ CO₂. What is its RQ?
transfer_answer: 0.70; this is compatible with predominantly lipid respiration but is still interpreted with the experimental assumptions.

subject: biology
title: Light-microscope prokaryotes: chains, sheaths and colonies
official_title: Observing and distinguishing bacteria and cyanobacteria under light microscope

source_verification.note: Official handbook activity objectives, materials and method inspected; this original theoretical exercise uses fictional data or specimen features and does not reproduce a laboratory protocol.

data: Bead-like trichome with occasional larger pale heterocysts
Unbranched trichomes within a conspicuous sheath; no heterocysts visible
Small rounded cells grouped in a mucilaginous colony
Separate short rods without visible chlorophyll pigmentation
scenario: For this exercise the cyanobacterial candidates are Anabaena, Lyngbya and Microcystis, as represented by the handbook slide set. Features support identification within that candidate set, not an unrestricted species diagnosis. The handbook spelling Lyngbia refers to Lyngbya.
tasks: Assign Anabaena to A, B or C.
Assign Lyngbya to A, B or C.
Assign Microcystis to A, B or C.
What specialised role is associated with the heterocysts of A?
Are cyanobacteria eukaryotic algae or bacteria?
worked_explanation: The feature combination and restricted candidate list distinguish the slides. Heterocysts support Anabaena, the sheathed trichome supports Lyngbya, and the mucilaginous colony supports Microcystis. Cyanobacteria belong among bacteria: the handbook comparison is between cyanobacteria and other bacteria, not two different domains. A routine light image does not resolve all internal ultrastructure.
common_error: Treating cyanobacteria as eukaryotes because they photosynthesise.
transfer_question: Why would failure to see a nucleus in one blurry light micrograph be insufficient, alone, to identify a cell as prokaryotic?
transfer_answer: An absent visible nucleus may reflect preparation, focus or resolution; identification needs additional reliable structural evidence.

subject: biology
title: Prokaryotic ultrastructure: a membrane is not a chloroplast
official_title: Use of electron micrographs to study morphological features of bacteria and cyanobacteria

source_verification.note: Official handbook activity objectives, materials and method inspected; this original theoretical exercise uses fictional data or specimen features and does not reproduce a laboratory protocol.

data: Nucleoid, ribosomes, surface wall; no membrane-bound nucleus
Nucleoid, ribosomes, wall and extensive internal photosynthetic thylakoid membranes; no chloroplast envelope
scenario: Fictional electron-image inventories compare a non-photosynthetic bacterial example with a cyanobacterial example. The assignment does not claim every non-cyanobacterial bacterium lacks photosynthetic membranes.
tasks: Which image fits the cyanobacterial example?
Name the DNA-containing region present in both.
Which listed structure is the site of protein synthesis?
Does F contain a membrane-bound chloroplast?
What observation supports classifying both as prokaryotic?
marks: DNA in a nucleoid without a membrane-bound nucleus.
worked_explanation: F has photosynthetic internal membranes but not a chloroplast. Cyanobacterial thylakoids are inside a prokaryotic cell; a chloroplast is a membrane-bounded organelle of a eukaryotic cell. Both examples share a nucleoid and ribosomes. Additional evidence would be required for an unrestricted taxonomic identification.
common_error: Labelling any internal photosynthetic membrane system as a chloroplast.
transfer_question: An electron image shows a nucleus and chloroplasts. Does it fit either of these prokaryotic examples?
transfer_answer: No. A membrane-bound nucleus supports eukaryotic organisation.

subject: biology
title: Seven organism cards: use observable characters
official_title: Observation of morphological features of Euglena, Paramecium, Amoeba, Ulva, Diatoms, Sargassum, Gelidium

source_verification.note: Official handbook activity objectives, materials and method inspected; this original theoretical exercise uses fictional data or specimen features and does not reproduce a laboratory protocol.

data: Siliceous cell wall consisting of overlapping parts
Brown branched thallus with air bladders
scenario: Cards are fictional representative drawings of Euglena, Paramecium, Amoeba, Ulva, a diatom, Sargassum and Gelidium. Use the full combination in the restricted set; colour is not the sole identification criterion.
tasks: Identify A.
Identify B.
Identify C.
Which card represents a diatom?
Match D, F and G to Ulva, Sargassum and Gelidium respectively.
marks: D = Ulva, F = Sargassum, G = Gelidium (all three required for this matching point).
worked_explanation: Locomotory structures separate A–C in this set. The silica wall is diagnostic for the diatom card. The thallus combinations separate the selected algae: green sheet, brown bladder-bearing branch system, and red cartilaginous branches. A table of features is stronger than relying on an isolated colour or habitat.
common_error: Calling Paramecium flagellated or treating the Sargassum air bladder as a reproductive structure.
transfer_question: A new card shows a flexible unicellular body, an eyespot and one conspicuous flagellum. Which candidate fits best?
transfer_answer: Euglena, within the given candidate set.

subject: biology
title: A plant-group sorting tray
official_title: Observation of morphological features of organisms of phyla Hepatophyta, Bryophyta, Anthocerophyta, Lycophyta, Pterophyta, Cycadophyta, Gnetophyta,Coniferophyta, Anthophyta and classes Monocotyledoneae and Dicotyledoneae

source_verification.note: Official handbook activity objectives, materials and method inspected; this original theoretical exercise uses fictional data or specimen features and does not reproduce a laboratory protocol.

data: Leafy moss gametophyte bearing a capsule on a seta
Fern frond with sori; vascular sporophyte
Needle leaves and cones; naked seeds
scenario: A fictional identification tray uses representative Marchantia, Pogonatum, Anthoceros, Nephrolepis, Pinus, a monocot and a dicot, all included in the official practical candidate range. Use the NIE grouping names for this syllabus exercise.
tasks: Identify the genus represented by A.
Assign B to Bryophyta or Anthocerophyta.
Identify the genus represented by C.
Which of D and E is a seed plant?
Classify F and G as monocot or dicot.
worked_explanation: Gemma cups support Marchantia and the horn-like sporophytes support Anthoceros. B has the moss capsule-on-seta pattern. Fern D is vascular but reproduces by spores without seeds; Pinus E is a naked-seeded gymnosperm. The flowering examples are distinguished by their supplied combinations, particularly cotyledon number.
common_error: Equating vascular tissue with seed production, thereby treating a fern as a seed plant.
transfer_question: An additional card has scale-like leaves, vascular tissue and strobili with spores, and is labelled Selaginella. Which handbook phylum contains it?

subject: biology
title: Four fungal drawings: reproductive structures matter
official_title: Observation of characteristic features of organisms of phyla Chytridiomycota, Zygomycota, Ascomycota and Basidiomycota

source_verification.note: Official handbook activity objectives, materials and method inspected; this original theoretical exercise uses fictional data or specimen features and does not reproduce a laboratory protocol.

data: Flagellated zoospore in a representative Allomyces life-cycle drawing
Coenocytic hyphae bearing sporangia; labelled Mucor
Septate hyphae with an upright conidiophore and chains of conidia; labelled Aspergillus
Mushroom gill bearing basidia and external basidiospores; labelled Agaricus
scenario: These fictional diagram descriptions follow the four representative genera and traditional phyla specified in the NIE handbook. No fungal cultivation is requested. Classification here follows the examination syllabus rather than claiming a current exhaustive fungal taxonomy.
tasks: Assign A to the handbook phylum.
Assign B to the handbook phylum.
Assign C to the handbook phylum.
Assign D to the handbook phylum.
Which drawing explicitly shows conidia rather than sporangiospores?
worked_explanation: The exercise deliberately pairs the source genera with reproductive features. Mucor sporangia enclose sporangiospores, whereas Aspergillus conidia are borne externally. Agaricus basidia bear basidiospores. Allomyces is assigned using the handbook grouping, whose traditional categories should not be silently replaced during syllabus revision.
common_error: Calling Aspergillus conidia spores inside a sporangium.
transfer_question: A diagram shows sac-like asci containing ascospores. Which of the four syllabus groups is indicated?

subject: biology
title: Build a defensible invertebrate key
official_title: Observation of morphological features of organisms of phyla Cnidaria, Platyhelminthes, Nematoda, Annelida, Mollusca, Arthropoda and Echinodermata

source_verification.note: Official handbook activity objectives, materials and method inspected; this original theoretical exercise uses fictional data or specimen features and does not reproduce a laboratory protocol.

data: Radial tentacles around mouth; cnidocytes shown in inset
Cylindrical unsegmented body tapering at ends
Muscular foot, visceral mass and mantle
Adult pentaradial body with tube feet
scenario: Fictional cards represent seven invertebrate phyla. The inset information is part of the supplied evidence. Construct classifications from positive distinguishing features rather than from assumed habitat.
tasks: Assign H to a phylum.
Assign P and N to their respective phyla.
Assign A to a phylum.
Assign M and R to their respective phyla.
State a mutually exclusive first key couplet that separates R from every other card.
marks: Jointed appendages present → R; jointed appendages absent → remaining cards.
worked_explanation: The key uses a character visible or explicitly described in the cards. A valid couplet gives mutually exclusive alternatives for the same character. E is Echinodermata from pentaradial symmetry with tube feet; it is not Cnidaria merely because both adults may be radial.
common_error: Using alternatives such as “lives in water” versus “has legs,” which are not mutually exclusive states of one character.
transfer_question: Which card is identified by tube feet together with adult pentaradial symmetry?

subject: biology
title: Vertebrates: discriminate with combined characters
official_title: Observation of characteristic features of organisms of classes Osteichthyes, Chondrichthyes, Amphibia, Reptilia, Aves and Mammalia

source_verification.note: Official handbook activity objectives, materials and method inspected; this original theoretical exercise uses fictional data or specimen features and does not reproduce a laboratory protocol.

data: Cartilaginous skeleton; separate exposed gill slits
Bony skeleton; gills covered by operculum
scenario: Six fictional specimen cards represent the classes named in the handbook. These are selected representative organisms, so do not generalise one example’s locomotion, habitat or reproductive mode to every member of its class.
tasks: Classify S.
Classify T.
Classify U.
Classify V and W.
Which card is diagnosed by mammary glands?
worked_explanation: The fish cards use skeleton and gill-cover features together. The other cards use characteristic integumentary features. Habitat is a weak classifier: aquatic mammals remain mammals and an amphibian is not identified merely by entering water.
common_error: Using “flies” as a unique bird character or “lives in water” as a unique fish character.
transfer_question: A flightless specimen bears feathers. Which class is indicated?
transfer_answer: Aves; flight is not required for membership.

subject: biology
title: Plant tissues: read the cell walls and contents
official_title: Identification of special characters of cell types of plant tissues using light microscope

source_verification.note: Official handbook activity objectives, materials and method inspected; this original theoretical exercise uses fictional data or specimen features and does not reproduce a laboratory protocol.

data: Features in a fictional prepared section
Living cells; thin primary walls; intercellular spaces
Living elongated cells; unevenly thickened non-lignified corners
Mature cells dead; very thick lignified walls and narrow lumens
Hollow elongated conducting elements with lignified walls
Sieve-tube elements with sieve plates and adjacent companion cells
scenario: Interpret a representative prepared plant section. The descriptions are a concrete feature table rather than a claim that every cell in a complex tissue has the same structure.
tasks: Identify P.
Identify C.
Identify S as a simple supporting tissue.
Identify the complex conducting tissue at X.
Identify the complex conducting tissue at F.
worked_explanation: Thin primary walls with living contents support parenchyma. Uneven flexible wall thickening is characteristic of collenchyma; heavy lignification supports sclerenchyma. Xylem and phloem are complex tissues, so individual cells within them can differ in viability and structure. Mature conducting vessel elements differ from adjacent xylem parenchyma.
common_error: Stating that every cell of xylem is dead because vessel elements are dead at maturity.
transfer_question: A fruit preparation shows isolated thick-walled, lignified, irregular cells. Which sclerenchyma cell type is suggested?

subject: biology
title: Four transverse sections: organ before plant group
official_title: Observation of transverse sections of primary stem and primary root of a monocot and a dicot

source_verification.note: Official handbook activity objectives, materials and method inspected; this original theoretical exercise uses fictional data or specimen features and does not reproduce a laboratory protocol.

data: Vascular bundles scattered through ground tissue
Vascular bundles in a ring; each has xylem inward and phloem outward
Central star-like xylem with phloem between arms; little central pith
Many xylem poles around a conspicuous central pith; distinct endodermis
scenario: Four fictional primary sections are selected typical monocot stem, dicot stem, dicot root and monocot root. Identify the organ as well as the group; the supplied representative patterns are not universal species diagnoses.
tasks: Identify A as the correct organ and group.
Identify B as the correct organ and group.
Identify C as the correct organ and group.
Identify D as the correct organ and group.
Name the tissue boundary surrounding the root stele.
worked_explanation: Scattered bundles and ring-arranged collateral bundles separate the selected stems. Root C has the typical central star-like xylem; D has polyarch xylem around pith. Roots have xylem and phloem arranged in separate alternating strands, so calling those root strands ordinary stem bundles obscures a useful anatomical difference.
common_error: Identifying a root as a stem simply because xylem and phloem are visible.
transfer_question: A primary section has central xylem and phloem alternating between its arms, surrounded by an endodermis. Is it more consistent with root or stem?

subject: biology
title: Woody stem: production direction and growth rings
official_title: Microscopic and macroscopic examination of secondary structure of dicotyledonous wood using transverse sections

source_verification.note: Official handbook activity objectives, materials and method inspected; this original theoretical exercise uses fictional data or specimen features and does not reproduce a laboratory protocol.

data: Thin dividing cylinder between secondary xylem and secondary phloem
Secondary conducting tissue immediately inside A
Secondary conducting tissue immediately outside A
Six complete annual rings outside the first-year boundary
scenario: A fictional woody dicot diagram explicitly states that each complete ring represents one annual growth cycle in this example. The first-year boundary is supplied to avoid confusing ring count with whole-tree age.
tasks: Identify A.
Identify B.
Identify C.
Name D relative to E.
How many annual growth cycles are represented by the six complete rings?
worked_explanation: Vascular cambium adds secondary xylem inward and secondary phloem outward. Sapwood is the younger outer wood involved in conduction; heartwood is older inner wood. Ring periodicity is explicitly assumed here because growth rings do not automatically equal years in every climate or species. The count describes the specified growth interval, not the age of every part of the plant.
common_error: Adding secondary xylem outside the vascular cambium, or estimating tree age without verifying annual periodicity.
transfer_question: A cambial cylinder forms three new xylem layers inward and phloem outward. Which meristem is responsible?
transfer_answer: Vascular cambium; cork cambium instead produces periderm tissues.

subject: biology
title: Leaf pores and woody-stem openings
official_title: Observation of the structure of stomata and lenticels through light microscope

source_verification.note: Official handbook activity objectives, materials and method inspected; this original theoretical exercise uses fictional data or specimen features and does not reproduce a laboratory protocol.

scenario: Compare a fictional leaf peel and a secondary-stem section, as in the handbook practical. The count is supplied to practise density; it is not a real species measurement.
tasks: Name L.
Name W.
Which cells regulate the aperture of L?
Calculate stomatal density in the leaf field.
State one shared role of L and W.
marks: Gas exchange between internal tissues and the atmosphere.
worked_explanation: The leaf opening has guard cells; the woody-stem opening has loosely packed complementary cells. Density is count/area = 24/0.12 = 200 stomata mm⁻². Lenticels lack a guard-cell aperture mechanism equivalent to a stoma. A single field estimates that sampled area and does not establish the entire leaf mean.
common_error: Calling a lenticel a pair of guard cells, or reporting stomatal count as a density without area.
transfer_question: A second field contains 18 stomata over 0.10 mm². What is its density?

subject: biology
title: Plasmolysis graph and the supplied solute-potential table
official_title: Determination of solute potential of epidermal peels of Rhoeo (Tradescantia)

source_verification.note: Official handbook activity objectives, materials and method inspected; this original theoretical exercise uses fictional data or specimen features and does not reproduce a laboratory protocol.

scenario: Fictional Tradescantia epidermal-cell counts follow the handbook percentage-plasmolysis method. The potential values shown are the handbook lookup values, not invented measurements. Use the 50% plasmolysis criterion as an estimate of the median cell solute potential.
tasks: Calculate percentage plasmolysis at 0.35 mol dm⁻³.
Identify the concentration giving 50% plasmolysis.
Estimate the tissue cell solute potential using the supplied table.
What is the approximate pressure potential of a cell at incipient plasmolysis?
Why does 50% tissue plasmolysis not mean every cell has identical solute potential?
marks: Cells differ, so the 50% criterion estimates a representative median rather than a value shared by all cells.
worked_explanation: Percentage plasmolysis = plasmolysed/total × 100. At the 50% criterion the corresponding sucrose concentration is 0.30 mol dm⁻³, with a supplied solute potential of −820 kPa. At incipient plasmolysis pressure potential is approximately zero, enabling the equilibrium comparison. The tissue estimate must not be described as an exact determination for every cell.
common_error: Using the zero-change potato-strip criterion instead of the 50% plasmolysis criterion, or dropping the negative potential sign.
transfer_question: Another field has 36 plasmolysed cells out of 80. What percentage is plasmolysed?

subject: biology
title: Potato length change: estimate tissue water potential
official_title: Determination of water potential of petioles of Alocasia/ potato strips

source_verification.note: Official handbook activity objectives, materials and method inspected; this original theoretical exercise uses fictional data or specimen features and does not reproduce a laboratory protocol.

scenario: Fictional potato-strip mean lengths represent the handbook length-change variant of Practical 21. Matched strips reached an approximate equilibrium. Potential values are supplied handbook lookup entries; the data do not use a mass-change method.
tasks: Calculate percentage length change at 0.15 mol dm⁻³.
Calculate percentage length change at 0.30 mol dm⁻³.
Identify the zero-change concentration.
Estimate the initial tissue water potential.
At 0.15 mol dm⁻³, state the net direction of water movement consistent with the elongation.
worked_explanation: Use (final − initial)/initial × 100: +3/50 × 100 = +6%, and −1.5/50 × 100 = −3%. Zero mean length change occurs at 0.25 mol dm⁻³, giving an approximate tissue water potential of −680 kPa using the supplied table. This is a water-potential estimate; it is not automatically the cells’ solute potential because tissue cells may have positive pressure potential.
common_error: Equating zero length change with 50% plasmolysis, or reporting the estimate as solute potential without accounting for pressure potential.
transfer_question: A 40.0 mm strip ends at 39.2 mm. Find percentage length change.

subject: biology
title: Potometer capillary geometry and the uptake proxy
official_title: Determination of rate of transpiration from leaves and shoots using a potometer

source_verification.note: Official handbook activity objectives, materials and method inspected; this original theoretical exercise uses fictional data or specimen features and does not reproduce a laboratory protocol.

scenario: Fictional potometer records use the same intact leafy shoot, with temperature, light and humidity held constant. Internal capillary area is given directly, so no radius estimate is needed. The apparatus measures water uptake.
tasks: Calculate water uptake volume in still air.
Calculate uptake rate in moving air.
Calculate the ratio of moving-air to still-air uptake rates.
State one reason uptake is not exactly equal to transpiration.
Explain the observed response to moving air in terms of the leaf boundary layer.
marks: Some absorbed water is retained or used in growth/metabolism rather than lost by transpiration.
Moving air reduces the humid boundary layer and helps maintain a water-vapour gradient.
worked_explanation: Volume displaced = capillary area × distance. Still-air uptake is 0.50 × 30 = 15 mm³, or 3 mm³ min⁻¹; moving-air uptake is 0.50 × 50/5 = 5 mm³ min⁻¹. The ratio is 5/3. The comparison supports a wind effect under the controlled conditions, but the reading remains an uptake proxy rather than direct measurement of every water molecule lost.
common_error: Using distance/time as a volume rate without multiplying by the capillary area.
transfer_question: Another calibrated capillary has area 0.20 mm² and bubble travel 45 mm in 3 min. Find uptake rate.

title: Heart model: follow the vessel, not oxygen content alone
official_title: Describing the organization of circulatory system of man using specimens/models/ diagrams

source_verification.note: Official handbook activity objectives, materials and method inspected; this original theoretical exercise uses fictional data or specimen features and does not reproduce a laboratory protocol.

data: Connection in a fictional heart model
Leaves right ventricle and goes to lungs
Returns from lungs to left atrium
Leaves left ventricle for systemic circulation
Returns systemic blood to right atrium
Wall of left ventricle visibly thicker than right
scenario: Use a model showing complete mammalian double circulation. Artery and vein are defined by direction relative to the heart, not by whether blood is oxygenated.
tasks: Name V1.
Name V2.
Name V3.
Which atrioventricular valve lies between left atrium and left ventricle?
Explain the thicker wall at W.
marks: Pulmonary artery (pulmonary trunk accepted for the initial vessel).
The left ventricle must generate the higher pressure needed for systemic circulation.
worked_explanation: Right ventricle → pulmonary artery → lungs → pulmonary veins → left atrium is the pulmonary route. Left ventricle → aorta → systemic tissues → systemic veins → right atrium completes the systemic route. The pulmonary artery carries relatively deoxygenated blood despite being an artery. Wall thickness reflects pressure demand, not a requirement to pump a greater long-term flow than the right ventricle.
common_error: Calling V1 a vein because its blood is relatively deoxygenated, or claiming the ventricles normally have unequal long-term outputs.
transfer_question: Which vessels deliver oxygenated blood directly to the heart muscle itself?

title: Breathing and pulse: normalise unequal count windows
official_title: Explaining the structure of human respiratory system using models or diagrams and observations of effects of exercise on respiratory rate and pulse rate

source_verification.note: Official handbook activity objectives, materials and method inspected; this original theoretical exercise uses fictional data or specimen features and does not reproduce a laboratory protocol.

scenario: Analyse a fictional, already completed teacher-supervised exercise demonstration; no exercise is requested of the reader. Different observation windows make direct comparison of counts misleading.
tasks: Calculate resting respiratory rate.
Calculate post-exercise respiratory rate.
Calculate the increase in pulse rate from rest to post-exercise.
Name the respiratory structure where most gas exchange occurs.
State one reason these observations do not prove the exact cause of a change in an untested individual.
marks: They are observations from one fictional participant; individual factors or unmeasured variables remain, so broad causal/clinical conclusions are unsupported.
worked_explanation: Rest gives 80/5 = 16 breaths min⁻¹; post-exercise gives 84/3 = 28. Pulse increases by 120 − 72 = 48 beats min⁻¹. These responses are consistent with increased gas exchange and transport demands during exercise. Recovery values move towards baseline, but this small table is not a fitness test or diagnosis.

tasks: Name A.

Name C.
Name D.
State the principal hormone secreted by E.
worked_explanation: Sperm develop within seminiferous tubules, mature in the epididymis and travel through the vas deferens. Sertoli cells support developing germ cells within tubules. title: Sterilisation choices: a paper-based matching exercise
official_title: Sterilization of water, culture media, glassware, heat labile substances and inoculating needles

source_verification.note: Official handbook activity objectives, materials and method inspected; this original theoretical exercise uses fictional data or specimen features and does not reproduce a laboratory protocol.

data: Heat-labile solution suitable for membrane filtration
Work surface with visible soil; disinfection is intended
scenario: This is a theoretical selection exercise, not instructions to operate equipment or handle microbes. Match broad method categories from the handbook. No temperatures, durations or practical steps are supplied.
tasks: Choose the handbook sterilisation method category for A.
Choose the category for B.
Choose the category for C.
Choose the category for D.
Does a disinfected surface automatically meet the definition of sterilisation?
marks: Dry heat in a hot-air oven.
No; disinfection does not necessarily eliminate all viable microorganisms, including resistant spores.
worked_explanation: The appropriate method depends on material stability and the intended outcome. Dry glass tolerates dry heat; an aqueous medium is suited to moist heat; a compatible heat-sensitive solution can be filtered. Filtration removes organisms rather than necessarily killing them. Surface disinfection must not be advertised as guaranteed sterilisation.
common_error: Choosing heat for a heat-labile substance or treating “disinfected” and “sterile” as synonyms.
transfer_question: Why is filtration a different control mechanism from thermal killing?
transfer_answer: Filtration physically removes microorganisms from a compatible liquid; thermal treatment acts by heat-induced inactivation.

title: Colony records: morphology is not species identity

source_verification.note: Official handbook activity objectives, materials and method inspected; this original theoretical exercise uses fictional data or specimen features and does not reproduce a laboratory protocol.

data: No visible colonies in the supplied image
scenario: Analyse fictional photographs from an already completed, supervised teaching demonstration. All cultures remain outside this exercise. No medium recipe, inoculation or incubation instructions are included. “Morphotype” means an appearance class, not an identified species.
tasks: Calculate total recorded colonies on sample 1.
How many morphotypes were recorded for sample 1?
State the result for the uninoculated control.
Does one colony necessarily represent one original microbial cell?
Can the cream colonies be assigned to a microbial species from colour and shape alone?
marks: No visible colonies in the supplied observation.
No; a colony may arise from a cell cluster or other colony-forming unit.
No; morphology alone is insufficient for reliable species identification.
worked_explanation: Sample 1 has 18 + 6 = 24 visible colonies in two appearance categories. The blank control supplies a check for visible background contamination under the stated observation conditions; it does not prove absence of every viable organism. Counts on these teaching plates cannot yield original sample concentration without suitable quantitative sampling/dilution information.
common_error: Reporting two morphotypes as proof of exactly two species, or converting counts to cells per millilitre without a sampled volume.
transfer_question: A photo has 9 small circular colonies and 5 large irregular colonies. Give total count and number of recorded morphotypes.
transfer_answer: 14 colonies; two recorded morphotypes. Neither value alone establishes the number of species.

subject: biology
title: Disinfectant comparison: counts, controls and restrained claims
official_title: Use of alcohol and other disinfectants to control microorganisms

source_verification.note: Official handbook activity objectives, materials and method inspected; this original theoretical exercise uses fictional data or specimen features and does not reproduce a laboratory protocol.

scenario: Use fictional closed-plate photograph counts from the handbook-style treated-versus-untreated comparison. Groups had matched exposure and observation conditions. No disinfectant formulation, microbial cultivation, exposure procedure or operational parameters are supplied.
tasks: Calculate the mean control count.
Calculate the mean treated count.
Calculate percentage reduction relative to the control mean.
Does this result establish that the treated group was sterile?
Name one design feature, in addition to matching exposure, needed for a fair comparison.
marks: No; visible colonies remained and reduced counts are not sterilisation evidence.
Same disinfectant concentration between treated replicates, or matched medium/observation duration/plate area (any one justified controlled condition).
worked_explanation: Means are (30 + 34)/2 = 32 and (6 + 10)/2 = 8. Reduction = (32 − 8)/32 × 100 = 75%. This measures relative reduction in the fictional visible-colony outcome, not the percentage of all microbes killed or universal product effectiveness. The original handbook comparison is based on colony counts, so a disc-diffusion zone has not been substituted.
common_error: Calling a 75% colony-count reduction “75% of all microorganisms killed,” or claiming sterility.
transfer_question: Another matched comparison has mean counts 50 untreated and 15 treated. What is the relative reduction?
transfer_answer: (50 − 15)/50 × 100 = 70%; this is a reduction in the measured colony outcome under those conditions.
